decisions.reason: The Korean specifies that he rose from his seat; BASE preserves that physical detail.
The Korean image is a voice digging into her ear; SOL’s “reached” drops that forceful image.
BASE preserves the hand stopping in midair and her turning away; SOL weakens both physical details.
“Her” clearly refers to Ju Hwaran, and SOL keeps the meaning without needless repetition.
SOL drops the faint quality of his smile.
SOL keeps the duration, wandering, and countless defeated enemies in natural prose.
“History, past and present” preserves the contrast between past and current history.
The Korean points to “that child”; SOL changes the demonstrative to “this.”
“Also” is consistent with the preceding statement that he knew the answer.
“Sham monk” carries the Korean’s disparaging 땡중, and the recast keeps the story’s sense.
SOL preserves her pause and careful question without changing the beat.
The question still asks whether Hong Dao is the person being discussed.
“Sham monk” preserves the Korean’s disparaging label.
The friendship’s wide renown is unchanged.
SOL keeps his fiery temper, the imbalance of enemies to friends, and Hong Dao’s calming role.
“His foul temper” clearly refers to Jeok Cheongang and avoids needless repetition.
The Korean says Hong Dao was respected throughout the Murim; SOL replaces the established term with “martial artists everywhere.”
“A wondrous thing to watch” preserves the sense of his uncanny skill.
The Korean notes that the story began suddenly; SOL drops that timing detail.
The Korean describes the Dharma King as a symbolic figure; SOL changes this to a figure of importance.
“Sham monk” preserves the source’s disparaging reference, and “told me something” keeps the meaning.
SOL preserves the memory etched deep in his mind in a tighter phrasing.
The recollection and the friend’s death are preserved in natural English.

“Take the existence seriously” preserves the meaning of beginning to pay serious attention.
“Turbulent darkness” naturally conveys the Korean’s disordered darkness, and the reference to the conversation is clear from context.
The phrasing preserves his held breath and its release.
The expected brief brilliance and fading remain intact.
The star’s clear northern light and persistence are preserved.
The Korean says the star’s size grew; SOL changes that to its strength.
The Korean identifies both Jeok Cheongang and Jin Taekyung; SOL omits their names from this narrated milestone.

SOL preserves that no one answered and Jeok Cheongang did not wait for a reply.
“Taken under my wing” adds a protective mentoring relationship; the Korean only says he kept the brat by his side.

The prediction and its emphasis on the Morning Star’s enduring light are preserved.
The shocked onlookers’ open-mouthed reaction is unchanged.
“Someone they all knew well” preserves the revelation’s familiarity.

SOL retains the shock’s measure against what they could imagine.
SOL keeps Hong Dao’s prediction and the Morning Star’s lasting light; the emphatic fragment is natural.

“Barely past twenty” preserves the age, while the calamity’s effect on the land remains.
“Whoosh” naturally conveys the Korean sound effect.
The gust of wind and rain opening the door amid the silence is preserved.
The wind and rain remain as fierce as before, and no one speaks.
The group’s shared turn toward the darkness and lingering shock are preserved.
The source evokes the place where the star had stayed before passing on; “where a star had been moments ago” changes the image.
“Toward” keeps the parallel direction of their gaze.
담담하게 describes a calm, matter-of-fact delivery; “quietly” changes the manner.
“Jeok Cheongang himself” preserves the emphasis on his initial skepticism.
“Practically an infant” preserves the rhetorical contrast with the calamity.
Naming Jeok Cheongang avoids an unnecessary shift to an implicit subject in this reflective passage.
The new star’s role as a guide through future darkness is preserved.
“Granted” naturally conveys Heaven allowing him this one light.
The Korean compares one star shining in darkness; SOL changes it to plural stars and replaces darkness gathering with waiting.
“Dared touch him” naturally keeps the source’s claim that darkness could not approach him.
The hypothetical day and the assurance that it is not this time are preserved.
The absence of complete darkness and the Morning Star’s greatest brilliance remain intact.

The long-past point of weighing right and wrong is preserved in a natural recast.
SOL retains the judgment that there is no justice in Murim or the wider world.
The source describes an incomprehensible series of events; SOL reduces this to events and drops their serial nature.
The Korean says growing old also means growing numb; SOL drops the additive “also.”
The cheapness of death and the people leaving one by one are preserved.
“What he had left” naturally preserves what he still wanted to protect.

“Unknown territory” is a natural rendering of an unfamiliar, secret-filled place.

The already-raging, overwhelming storm and indistinguishable foes are preserved.
The unavoidable need to face what comes is preserved without changing the meaning.

SOL preserves the direction, recalled layout, and approaching eunuch in natural narration.

The usefulness of the foul weather is unchanged.
The door’s groan being swallowed by the rain is preserved.
The Korean registers one presence upstairs; SOL makes that presence specifically a person.
The Korean compares his teeth with those of an ordinary person of the era; SOL changes the comparison to most people.
The empty room’s lack of even a candle or furniture remains clear.
“Humble setting” fits the source’s modest description without intensifying it to squalor.

The teasing inference that other things are unacceptable is preserved.
The implication that the conversation will end quickly remains intact.
